Bro the numbers you're talking are on the power plant order of magnitude.

So yeah you could have that kind if wattage in a wire but it'd be one big ass cable.

You're getting a lot of answers from people who only seem to have an elementary understanding of how power generation and transmission works.

So - I'll try to help out as best I can. Since you didn't specify, I'm assuming you are talking DC power through some sort T-line. If this is the case, then the voltage and current specified are massive. It really isn't practical because of the high current (10kA is a shitload). The caviat of high current is high loss. That is to say, the power lost during transmission is solved from the equation P=I^2 * R where I is current and R is resistance of the T-line.

In AC the voltage and current constantly change signs, usually at 60hz or 120hz or in that ballpark. What AC power generation also takes advantage of is 3 phase power, which is a whole other thread I could go on about, but basically 3 phase power lets you transfer power without a neutral line.

Since the power is generated in 3-ph AC typically, transformers are used to step this voltage up or down. 10kV and 10kA would refer to the magnitude of the phasor sine waves representing one phase. This means that you would have a 100-300MW power plant. Not only that, but having a voltage as high as 10kV magnitude will basically ensure that your current is lower than 10kA because of the way step up and step down transformers work. When you want more voltage out of a sine wave you have to sacrifice current - there's no way around it.

So the answer is yes, very possible - but not practical in any context I can think of.
Also don't ever tell an engineer that voltage is 'inside' the wire. Voltage is across two points, current is through a point
